title: Vasudeva in the jail cell
hookLine: a prisoner looks at the bars of his cell and sees Krishna
carry: vasudeva is everything, even the bars

cards: A jail cell in Calcutta, and a prisoner waiting for his trial. He'd been a writer and a political leader, arguing hard for India's freedom from British rule, and now he's accused in a bombing case.
He's allowed very little. One of the few things he has is a copy of the Bhagavad Gita. Later, after he walked out free, he gave a speech about what happened to him in that cell.
His name was Aurobindo Ghose. People came to know him as Sri Aurobindo.

teach.h: IN JAIL, HE WAS GIVEN THE GITA.
teach.b: In the speech, Aurobindo says he had asked God for guidance before his arrest, and in jail he felt the answer came. He was given the Gita, and he was asked, as he tells it, to live what it teaches, not just read it.
Then something changed in how he saw.

teach.h: THE WALLS, THE TREE, THE BARS: VASUDEVA.
teach.b: He looked at the walls that held him, and they were no longer walls. It was Vasudeva, a name for Krishna, standing around him. The tree in the yard: Vasudeva.
The bars of the cell, the grating on the door: Vasudeva again. He looked at the other prisoners, thieves and men accused of murder, and found Vasudeva in them too.

teach.h: EVEN THE PRISONERS. EVEN THE PROSECUTOR.
teach.b: Even in court, looking at the prosecutor arguing to convict him, he saw the same presence. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, said plainly: God is in everything and everyone.
The Gita puts it in three words, vasudevah sarvam, Vasudeva is everything, and Krishna says the one who sees him in everything, and everything in him, is never lost to him.
Aurobindo is describing what it was like when that line stopped being an idea. And notice where it happened. Not in a temple.
In a jail, among accused men, facing the man trying to convict him.
It's also how many Hindus read the everyday namaste, palms together: a bow to the divine in the other person, whoever they are.

how: Some followers of Sri Aurobindo read his speeches, letters and books as part of daily practice, and his ashram in Puducherry and centers elsewhere hold collective meditation and study of his writings.

s: Aurobindo's vision of Vasudeva everywhere came in a temple on a mountain
by his own account, it came in a jail cell, while he awaited trial.
he says he saw Vasudeva even in the prisoners around him
thieves and men accused of murder, and later the magistrate and prosecutor too.
the Gita teaches that God is found only in temples
Krishna says the one who sees him in everything, and everything in him, is never lost to him: Vasudeva is everything.

games.q: you're on trial, and the prosecutor is arguing to convict you. you've been living with the Gita in your cell. what does Aurobindo say he saw when he looked at that man?
o: Vasudeva, the same presence he saw in the walls and the prisoners.
nothing at all; he kept his eyes on the floor.
games.why: by his own account, even the prosecutor was Vasudeva to him: the Gita's 'Vasudeva is everything', tested on the hardest person in the room.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something ordinary in front of you, a wall, a window frame, a cup, and look at it slowly before moving on to the next thing, and the next.
If you pray, hold each one as Aurobindo held the walls of his cell, as a place where God is; if you don't, give each thing the attention you'd give something precious.
Last, bring to mind one person you find hard, and hold them there too, and in your mind fold your hands to them: namaste.

wordCard.voice: Aurobindo. The writer and freedom fighter who, by his own account, saw Krishna in the walls, the bars and the prisoners of his jail.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Vasudeva, a name for Krishna, the name Aurobindo uses for what he saw in his cell.
